title: The City and Its Challenges
description: Ten calm stories, letters and reports about city life and how people solve its problems: a bike lane, a new park, noise between neighbors, sorting waste, a square repaired by residents, bus changes, a city app, students at City Hall, a discovery under a street and a dinner on a quiet street.

lessons.title: A Bike Lane on Oak Street
lessons.summary: A narrow city street gets a temporary bike lane, and after six months the city makes it official.
lessons.text:
Oak Street is one of the busiest streets in Riverton, and it is also one of the narrowest. Every morning, cars, buses and even a few semis drive down this narrow street. A semi is a very large truck, and when a semi passes, people on bikes have almost no space.

Last spring, the city's transportation commissioner, Anna Ruiz, suggested a bike lane on Oak Street. To make room for it, the street would lose 40 parking spaces. Not everyone liked the idea. Its opponents, mostly drivers and a few shop owners, said that customers would stop coming if they could not park. "If the city had asked us first, we would have felt better about it," one shop owner said.

Bike advocates, on the other hand, said the lane was really needed. "An advocate is someone who speaks for other people," said Ben Carter, who leads a local bike group. "We speak for everyone who is afraid to ride here."

The commissioner listened to both sides. Instead of building a permanent lane right away, she decided to try a temporary one. In June, workers painted a temporary lane and put up plastic posts along it. The drivers of semis were asked to use a wider street nearby. The city said the temporary lane would stay for 6 months, and after that the city council would decide.

The results were clear. The number of people riding bikes on Oak Street went up by 60 percent, and accidents decreased by a third. The percentage of shop customers who arrived by bike grew from 5 percent to 15 percent, and sales did not decrease. Even some opponents changed their minds. "I should have waited before I complained," the shop owner said. "My sales are the same, and the street is quieter."

Last week, the lane got the council's approval. With this approval, the lane is now officially part of Oak Street. The commissioner said that workers would be replacing the plastic posts with a low wall in the fall. "By next summer, we will have built 2 more lanes like this one," she said.

Questions:
Why is Oak Street difficult for people on bikes?
It is busy and narrow, and even semis drive down it.
What did the opponents of the bike lane say?
They said that customers would stop coming if they could not park.
Why did the commissioner try a temporary lane first?
She wanted to see the results before the city built a permanent lane.
How did the number of accidents change?
Accidents decreased by a third.
How did the percentage of customers who arrived by bike change?
The percentage grew from 5 percent to 15 percent.
What happened last week?
The lane got the council's approval, so it is now officially part of Oak Street.

lessons.title: The New Park
lessons.summary: An empty lot becomes a small park, and the writer's dog wins a medal at the opening.
lessons.text:
When I was a child, there was an empty lot at the end of my street. It was full of old tires and broken glass, and my parents never let me play there. Most of my childhood memories are of gray walls and busy roads. As a child, I often wished we had a park nearby.

Two years ago, the city decided to turn the lot into a park. Last Saturday, the new park opened, and everyone on our street was invited to the opening. I was invited too, of course, and I brought my dog, Max.

The park is small, but it is very attractive. There are young trees, a path and benches, and along the path there are big pots full of red and yellow flowers, which make the path even more attractive. Each pot was painted by children from the school nearby. At night, the park is lit by solar lights. The solar lights collect energy from the sun during the day, so the city does not have to pay for their power.

There is also a special area for dogs, which is ideal for people like me who live in small apartments. Max loves to run, and now he has an ideal place to do it, only 5 minutes from home.

As part of the opening, the park held a small dog show. Dogs of every breed were invited: big ones, small ones and mixed ones like Max, who is not any particular breed. A woman with 3 dogs of the same breed told me that she had been waiting for a dog area for years. Every dog in the show received a medal. Max got a medal for "the happiest dog." It was not a real competition, but I put his medal on our kitchen wall anyway.

Walking home that evening, I thought about my childhood again. If there had been a park like this when I was young, I would have played there every day. I wish it had been here 30 years ago. But the children growing up on this street today will have different childhood memories: trees, flowers in painted pots, solar lights and a happy dog with a medal.

Questions:
What was at the end of the street when the writer was a child?
There was an empty lot full of old tires and broken glass.
Who was invited to the opening of the park?
Everyone on the street was invited.
What do the solar lights do?
They collect energy from the sun during the day and light the park at night.
Why is the dog area ideal for the writer?
The writer lives in a small apartment, and Max loves to run.
What did Max get at the dog show?
He got a medal for "the happiest dog."
What would the writer have done if there had been a park when the writer was young?
The writer would have played there every day.

lessons.title: Noise from Above
lessons.summary: A tired baker finally talks to the family upstairs, and they settle a noise problem in ten minutes.
lessons.text:
I have lived in my apartment for 8 years, and for most of that time it was a quiet place. The people on the floor above me were an older couple who hardly made a sound. When they moved away last fall, a young family moved in: Lisa and Mark Chen and their 2 small boys.

I work at a bakery, so my alarm clock rings at 4 every morning, and I go to bed at 9. But at 9, the boys were constantly running, jumping and dropping things. I could hardly sleep. I lay in bed looking at the clock: 9:30, 10:00, 10:30. The silence I used to love was gone.

At first, I did nothing. I did not want a dispute with the family. I had seen a dispute between two people in my old building, and it had lasted for years. The discord had made the whole building unhappy, and I did not want that kind of discord here.

After a month, however, I was so tired that I constantly made small mistakes at work. I knew I had to talk to the Chen family somehow. One evening, I knocked on their door. I was nervous, but Lisa smiled and invited me in. I explained that I went to bed early because of my job.

Lisa looked surprised. "We had no idea," she said. "We didn't know that the noise reached your apartment. You should have told us earlier!" She was right. If I had talked to them in the first week, I would have slept much better for a month.

It took us only 10 minutes to settle the problem. The boys would play in their bedroom at the back after 8, and the family would put soft mats on the living room floor. In return, I promised to tell them right away if there was a problem again. Somehow, everything felt easy once we were talking.

Now, when I go to bed, there is silence again, or almost silence. Sometimes I hear a small laugh, but it does not bother me. In fact, it is a comfort to know that the people above me are kind. It is also a comfort to know that I can knock on their door. The only thing I regret is waiting so long. I regret those tired weeks, but I learned something: you can settle most problems between neighbors with a simple conversation.

Questions:
Why does the writer go to bed at 9?
The writer works at a bakery, and the writer's alarm clock rings at 4 every morning.
Why didn't the writer want a dispute?
The writer had seen a dispute in an old building, and the discord had lasted for years.
What did Lisa say when she heard about the problem?
She said they had no idea and that the writer should have told them earlier.
How did they settle the problem?
The boys agreed to play in their back bedroom after 8, and the family agreed to put soft mats on the living room floor.
What does the writer regret?
The writer regrets waiting so long before talking to the family.

lessons.title: Two Emails About Our Waste
lessons.summary: A building manager explains, in two emails, how residents can sort their waste better.
lessons.text:
Subject: Sorting our waste

Dear residents,

As many of you know, our building has a problem with the waste room. Many bags are sorted badly, and the city has warned us twice. If this continues, the building will have to pay a fine. So I would like to give you a short explanation of the rules, with a few tips.

Bottles and cans: please crush them before you put them in the blue bin. A crushed bottle takes up much less space than a full one. If everyone crushed their bottles, we would need half as many bins.

Tubes: empty tubes, for example from toothpaste or face cream, cannot go in the blue bin, because they are hard to clean. Please put all tubes in the gray bin.

Coffee filters: used coffee filters and coffee go in the green bin with the food waste. Used filters are wet and dirty, so they do not belong with clean paper.

I have attached a list of what goes in each bin. Please print the attached list and put it on the inside of a kitchen cabinet door, so that you see it every day. Some residents also keep a small bag for bottles and cans in the cabinet under the sink.

Our goal is to eliminate mistakes by the end of the year. I know we cannot eliminate every mistake in one week. In the end, it is a question of habit. Once sorting becomes a habit, you will not even think about it. It took me about 2 weeks to build the habit myself.

If anything in this explanation is not clear, please call me or leave a note under my door.

Thank you,
Diane Wood, Building Manager

Subject: Good news

Dear residents,

Thank you all! Last month, the city checked our waste room again, and this time only 2 bags were sorted badly. That is the best result we have ever had. I can see that many of you have crushed your bottles and put the list in your cabinet. I hope that by spring we will have eliminated mistakes completely.

Diane Wood

Questions:
Why did the building manager write the first email?
Many bags were sorted badly, and the city had warned the building twice.
Why should residents crush bottles and cans?
A crushed bottle takes up much less space.
Where do empty tubes go?
All tubes go in the gray bin.
What did Diane send with her first email?
She attached a list of what goes in each bin.
What does Diane say about habit?
She says that once sorting becomes a habit, you will not even think about it.

lessons.title: The Pink Benches of Lincoln Square
lessons.summary: Residents repair an old square themselves, and the city thanks them for their work.
lessons.text:
For many years, Lincoln Square was not a place where people wanted to spend time. The benches were broken, the ground was rough and uneven, and the few trees looked tired. Most people walked through the square quickly and never sat down.

Last year, a group of residents started an initiative to repair the square themselves. The initiative was led by Rosa Mendez, a retired art teacher who has lived next to the square for 40 years. "I was tired of complaining," she said. "I decided that we should do something instead." The city agreed to pay for the materials, as long as the residents did the work.

Every Saturday for 3 months, about 30 volunteers met in the square. A local store gave them tool kits, and each team received a kit with hammers, nails, gloves and paint. The volunteers built new benches from raw wood. Raw wood is rough, so they had to make every board smooth before they could paint it. Then they put the boards together with long nails. By the end of the project, they had used more than 5,000 nails.

Children joined a craft table, where they made colorful signs for the square. The craft table was run by Rosa herself. The children also chose the color for the benches: pink. "Pink is a happy color," said one 8-year-old girl. At first, some adults were not sure about pink benches. Afterwards, however, almost everyone agreed that the pink benches made the square look friendly and bright.

The project needed real commitment. Some volunteers came every single Saturday, even when it rained. "It was a big commitment," said one volunteer, "but I am happy that I said yes. I would have regretted it if I had stayed at home."

Afterwards, the city said that the residents had done work worth about $50,000. "Their time was very valuable to the city," the mayor said. But Rosa believes the most valuable result was something else. "We got to know each other," she said. "Now, when I sit on a pink bench, people stop and talk to me."

Questions:
What was Lincoln Square like before the project?
The benches were broken, the ground was rough, and people walked through it quickly.
Who led the initiative?
Rosa Mendez, a retired art teacher, led the initiative.
What was in each tool kit?
There were hammers, nails, gloves and paint.
Why did the volunteers have to work on the raw wood?
Raw wood is rough, so they had to make every board smooth.
What does Rosa think was the most valuable result?
She thinks the most valuable result was that people got to know each other.

lessons.title: What the New Bus System Means for You
lessons.summary: A newspaper explains how the city's new bus cards, discounts and downtown loop will work.
lessons.text:
On March 1, Riverton will start using a new system on all city buses. Many people have written to us with questions, so here is a short guide to the changes.

The biggest change is the way you pay. Until now, you had to pay with cash, and you had to have the exact amount, because drivers do not give change. Searching for the exact amount was a problem for many people. From March 1, you will simply tap a card on a card reader when you get on the bus. You can also tap your phone. Each tap is one transaction, and the price is always $2.

The new system also counts your rides automatically. After 30 transactions in one month, the rest of your rides that month are free. You do not need to do anything: the system does it automatically. For a person who rides to work and back every day, 30 transactions are the equivalent of about 2 weeks of rides, so the second half of the month is free.

There are also new discounts. Students in junior high and high school will get a 50 percent discount, and people over 65 will get the same discount. Junior high and high school students can get their cards at school. Other people can order a card online or buy one at the train station.

The second big change is a new downtown loop. Small electric buses will be running in a loop around the city center every 10 minutes, from 7 in the morning until 10 at night. The loop will connect the train station, the hospital, the library and the main shopping streets. Rides on the loop are free.

Will the changes have an immediate effect on traffic? The city does not expect an immediate change. "People need time to change their habits," said transportation commissioner Anna Ruiz. "But by the end of the year, we hope that 1,000 more people will have left their cars at home."

The city has also published a calendar of the changes. According to the calendar, the new card readers will be put on the buses in February, and the old machines will be removed in April. You can find the calendar on the city's website.

Questions:
Why was paying with cash a problem for many people?
They had to have the exact amount, because drivers do not give change.
How will people pay from March 1?
They will tap a card or a phone on a card reader.
What happens after 30 transactions in one month?
The rest of the rides that month are free.
Why is the second half of the month free for a person who rides to work and back every day?
For this person, 30 transactions are the equivalent of about 2 weeks of rides.
Who will get a 50 percent discount?
Students in junior high and high school and people over 65 will get the discount.
What is the downtown loop?
It is a free bus line that runs around the city center every 10 minutes.

lessons.title: The App That Fixes Streets
lessons.summary: A young developer builds a simple app for reporting street problems and learns from the people who use it.
lessons.text:
I am a developer, which means that I write computer programs for a living. Two years ago, I was walking home late at night when I noticed that 3 street lights on my block were broken. I wanted to report them, but the city's website was so confusing that I gave up after 20 minutes. I thought, "There must be an easier way." That night, I started writing a small app.

The idea was simple. If you see a problem, such as a broken light, a hole in the road or a full trash bin, you take a photo with your phone. The app adds your location automatically and sends the report to the right city office. For the map, I made a clear graphic with a different color for each kind of problem. A friend who designs graphics helped me make it look attractive.

I worked on the app every evening for 3 months. Sitting at my desk with my mouse and my keyboard, I tested every button again and again. I must have clicked my mouse a million times. Even so, the first version had a bug. When people took a photo at night, the app crashed. Fixing that bug took me a whole weekend. For a developer, there is always another bug to fix.

To explain how the app worked, I recorded a short video clip and shared it online. In the clip, I reported a broken bench in 30 seconds. The clip was watched 10,000 times in a week. After that, the city contacted me, because it needed a developer. They had tried to build a similar app with an external company, but the external company had asked for a large sum of money. The city offered me a much smaller sum to make my app official. I said yes.

What I enjoy most is the interaction with users. Every interaction teaches me something. An older man told me that the buttons were too small, so I made them bigger. A woman asked for a way to see when a problem was fixed, so I added that too.

Last year, people sent the city more than 8,000 reports through the app, and 90 percent of the problems were fixed within a month. My ultimate goal is simple: I want every resident to feel that the city listens to them. If I had given up that night, none of this would have happened.

Questions:
Why did the writer start writing the app?
The city's website was so confusing that the writer could not report the broken street lights.
What does the app do automatically?
It adds your location and sends the report to the right city office.
What was the bug in the first version?
The app crashed when people took a photo at night.
Why didn't the city use the external company?
The external company asked for a large sum of money.
What is the writer's ultimate goal?
The writer wants every resident to feel that the city listens to them.

lessons.title: Students at City Hall
lessons.summary: A class of secondary school students asks the city council for a safe place to cross the street, and the council agrees.
lessons.text:
Every year, Ms. Grant teaches her students at Riverton Secondary School about democracy. Usually they read about elections and the government. This year, she wanted them to see democracy in action, so she asked her class to choose a real problem in the city and try to solve it.

The students did not have to look far. In front of their school, there is a wide, busy road, and the closest safe place to cross is a quarter of a mile away. Many students cross in the middle of the road, and there have been several accidents. For the city, this road had always been a secondary problem, because no one had ever asked about it.

First, the students counted the cars regularly for 2 weeks. They stood by the road every morning and every afternoon, and they wrote down the numbers. Then they asked the city council for permission to speak at its next meeting. Permission was given, and 5 students prepared a short talk.

At the meeting, a student named Sam Ortiz spoke first. "Students cross this road regularly, 4 times a day," he said. "We urge you to build a safe crossing with lights in front of our school. We urge you to do it before someone is badly hurt." The council members listened and asked many questions.

Afterwards, a council member told the students that she was impressed. "People often think that democracy only happens during a presidential election, once every 4 years," she said. "But even in a presidential election, many people do not vote. Democracy happens here too, in small rooms like this one. Today's meeting is a good example." She also said that she wished more young people were engaged in city life.

A month later, the council voted to build the crossing. Workers will have finished it by the time the next school year starts. The students were proud, and they were even more engaged afterwards. Several of them now go to council meetings regularly.

At the end of the year, Ms. Grant asked the class what the moral of the story was. Sam answered, "The moral is that you have to show up. If we had stayed in our classroom, nothing would have changed." Ms. Grant said that today's students would be the leaders of tomorrow, and that this was the most important lesson about democracy.

Questions:
What did Ms. Grant want her students to see?
She wanted them to see democracy in action.
What problem did the students choose?
There was no safe place to cross the busy road in front of their school.
What did the students ask the council for?
They asked for permission to speak at its next meeting.
What did Sam urge the council to do?
He urged the council to build a safe crossing with lights in front of the school.
What was the moral of the story, according to Sam?
The moral is that you have to show up.

lessons.title: A Discovery Under Elm Street
lessons.summary: Workers find an old horse stable under a street, and researchers study it before the street opens again.
lessons.text:
Last spring, workers were replacing the old water pipes under Elm Street when they made an unexpected discovery. About 6 feet below the road, they found the walls of an old brick building. The work was stopped immediately, and the city called researchers from the local university.

The researchers studied the site closely for 6 weeks. They soon found traces of horses: old horseshoes, pieces of leather and traces of hay on the floor. The building had clearly been a stable. "About 140 years ago, horses pulled the city's first buses, so the bus company needed a large stable," explained Dr. Nora Kim, the researcher in charge. "This stable must have held about 50 horses."

The researchers dug very carefully, layer by layer. The sequence of the layers told them the story of the site. At the bottom was the stable floor. Above it, there was a layer of ash and broken bricks, so the stable must have burned at some point. Above that were the stones of the first road, and at the top was the modern road. Following this sequence, the researchers could put the events in the right order.

One small mystery remained for a few days: what had happened to the stable? The answer was found in a contemporary newspaper, which means a newspaper from the same time. According to this contemporary report, the stable burned in 1902, and no horses were hurt. Soon afterwards, the city built a road over it. So the mystery was solved.

Among the objects that were found, the most popular one was a leather belt with a metal buckle. Dr. Kim believes the belt belonged to one of the men who took care of the horses. "When you look closely at the belt, you can see where he made extra holes," she said. "He must have worn it for many years."

Now the pipes have been replaced, and the street is open again. The belt, the horseshoes and other objects will be shown at the city museum this fall. Next to the place where the stable was found, the city has put a small sign. "Without this discovery," Dr. Kim said, "we would never have known that this quiet street was once a busy place full of horses."

Questions:
What did the workers find under Elm Street?
They found the walls of an old brick building.
How did the researchers know the building was a stable?
They found traces of horses, such as horseshoes, leather and hay.
What did the sequence of layers tell the researchers?
It told them the story of the site, in the right order.
How was the mystery solved?
The answer was found in a contemporary newspaper from 1902.
What was the most popular object?
The most popular object was a leather belt with a metal buckle.

lessons.title: Dinner on Pine Street
lessons.summary: The residents of a busy street close it to cars for one evening and share a long dinner.
lessons.text:
Pine Street, where I live, is a short street with houses on both sides and a small temple at the corner. Every day, hundreds of cars use it to avoid the traffic on the main road. The cars have robbed our street of its quiet. Children do not play outside, and people hardly talk to each other.

Last summer, I asked the city for permission to close the street to cars for one evening and hold a dinner for everyone who lives there. To my surprise, the city said yes immediately. The only rule was that the street had to be open again by 11 at night.

Many people helped. The temple at the corner lent us 20 long tables and 100 chairs. The people from the temple also offered to bring rice and soup. My uncle Leo, who used to be a baker, said he would bake bread. On the day of the dinner, he arrived with 30 loaves of fresh bread in the back of his car. He also brought a big bread knife. "A good knife is the secret," my uncle said, while he cut the bread into thick pieces.

By 6 in the evening, the tables were full, and everyone was hungry. Some people had cooked at home, and others had brought fruit or cakes. A young musical group from the temple played quiet music. They were not professional musicians, but their musical evening was the best part of the night for many of us.

There was one small accident. My uncle was wearing his best white pants, and a child dropped a bowl of tomato soup on them. Uncle Leo just laughed. "Now my pants are red and white," he said, and he wore the same pants happily for the rest of the evening.

Nobody went home hungry. We talked until late, and I met people who had lived 3 houses away from me for 10 years. When the cars came back at 11, the street was clean and the tables were back at the temple.

The traffic still robs us of our quiet on most days. But now we know each other, and we have already chosen a date for next summer's dinner. If I had not asked the city that day, I would never have met half of my street.

Questions:
Why is Pine Street usually not quiet?
Hundreds of cars use it every day to avoid the traffic on the main road.
What did the temple lend for the dinner?
It lent 20 long tables and 100 chairs.
What did Uncle Leo bring?
He brought 30 loaves of fresh bread and a big bread knife.
What happened to Uncle Leo's white pants?
A child dropped a bowl of tomato soup on them.
Did anyone go home hungry?
No, nobody went home hungry.
What will the residents do next summer?
They will hold another dinner on the street.
